mcqs.question: What is the unit of deployment and billing on a FaaS platform?
options: The container image, regardless of how many functions it contains
mcqs.explanation: FaaS bills and deploys at the function level — each function is its own unit, unlike a VM or a long-running application process that bundles many endpoints together.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't a FaaS function have a listening process waiting for requests the way a traditional server does?
options: FaaS functions only run on a fixed daily schedule
Execution is triggered by events — an HTTP call, a queue message, a file upload — so nothing runs or costs money until a trigger fires
FaaS platforms don't support HTTP-triggered functions
A listening process is required but hidden from the developer
mcqs.explanation: The event-driven model is the core mechanic: the platform invokes your code on a trigger rather than your code sitting in a loop waiting for one. HTTP triggers are one of several supported trigger types, not an exception.

mcqs.question: A workload runs at high, constant volume 24/7. Why might pay-per-invocation billing be a poor fit compared to an always-on VM?
options: FaaS platforms cannot handle constant, high-volume traffic at all
Pay-per-invocation billing is always cheaper regardless of traffic pattern
At constant high volume, the per-invocation premium is effectively paid every second, eliminating the idle-time savings that make serverless cheap for spiky workloads
VMs can only be billed through fixed monthly contracts, never by the hour
mcqs.explanation: Serverless economics work because you don't pay for idle time; at sustained high volume there's no idle time to save, so a plain VM's steady per-hour rate usually undercuts the per-invocation premium.

mcqs.question: Why is storing a counter in a function's local memory between invocations unsafe?
options: Local memory is always encrypted, which adds unacceptable latency
Local memory is shared across every customer's functions, creating a security risk
FaaS platforms disable local memory access entirely
A function instance may be reused, frozen, or destroyed between calls, so there's no guarantee the next invocation sees the same memory
mcqs.explanation: The platform, not your code, decides whether an instance survives to serve the next invocation — any state that must persist needs an external store, not local memory.
